answer: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol): Polls devices for data. Uses MIB (Management Information Base). Versions: v1/v2c (community strings) and v3 (encrypted). Syslog: Centralized logging of device messages.
GET: Retrieve a value. GETNEXT: Get next value in MIB tree. GETBULK: Retrieve large amounts of data. SET: Modify a value. TRAP: Device sends unsolicited notification to manager.

Network flow monitoring protocol developed by Cisco. Collects IP traffic information (source/destination IP, ports, protocols, bytes). Used for bandwidth analysis, security monitoring, and capacity planning.
PRTG Network Monitor, Nagios, SolarWinds, Zabbix, LibreNMS, Cisco DNA Center. Provide dashboards, alerts, reports, and automated discovery of network devices.

UDP port 514. Provides event logging from network devices to a central server. Severity levels 0-7 (Emergency to Debug). Facility codes identify the source (e.g., local0-local7). Configurable with logging commands.
Enhances SNMP monitoring by providing data in a management console rather than polling network devices. Monitors traffic statistics, history, alarms, and events at Layer 1/2/3.
Network diagrams (logical and physical), IP address management (IPAM) documentation, device configurations, change management logs, business continuity plans, cable documentation.
Process for managing network changes: Request, Assessment, Approval, Implementation, Verification, Documentation. Follows ITIL framework. Minimizes disruption and provides rollback plans.
Tracks and manages device configurations. Backup configurations regularly. Use version control. Compare configurations to detect unauthorized changes. Tools: RANCID, Oxidized.
Bandwidth utilization, latency, jitter, packet loss, throughput, frame rate. Baseline normal performance for comparison. Threshold-based alerting for anomalies.
Time it takes for a packet to travel from source to destination. Affected by distance, processing delays, queuing delays, and transmission delays. Measured with ping and traceroute.
Variation in packet arrival time. Causes poor voice/video quality. Measured in milliseconds. Buffering and QoS can mitigate jitter. Real-time applications (VoIP) are sensitive to jitter.
Percentage of packets that fail to reach destination. Causes: congestion, faulty hardware, interference. Significant for real-time applications. Measured with ping, traceroute, or network monitors.

Bandwidth: Maximum capacity of a link (theoretical). Throughput: Actual amount of data transferred successfully in a given time. Throughput is always ≤ bandwidth due to overhead, latency, and congestion.

Traffic shaping: Controls data flow to prevent congestion. Rate limiting: Caps bandwidth for specific traffic or users. QoS (Quality of Service): Prioritizes critical traffic (VoIP, video) over best-effort.
Ping: Tests connectivity. Traceroute/Tracert: Shows path to destination. NSLookup/Dig: DNS resolution. Ipconfig/Ifconfig: IP configuration. Netstat: Active connections and listening ports.

Packet analyzer (network protocol analyzer). Captures and inspects packets in real-time. Filters using display filters (e.g., `ip.addr == 192.168.1.1`, `tcp.port == 80`). Used for deep network troubleshooting.
Traces the path packets take to a destination. Each router decrements TTL; when TTL reaches 0, ICMP Time Exceeded is sent back. Reveals hops, latency per hop, and potential bottlenecks.

Network scanner for discovery and security auditing. Port scanning (-p), OS detection (-O), version detection (-sV), script scanning (--script). Used for network inventory and vulnerability assessment.
Keep diagrams updated after every change. Label all cables and ports. Document IP assignments in a central database. Maintain configuration backups. Include physical location and contact information.

Analyze current and projected bandwidth usage. Account for growth (user count, applications, data volumes). Plan for redundancy and scalability. Use monitoring data to forecast when upgrades are needed.

Distributes network traffic across multiple servers. Methods: Round-robin, least connections, IP hash, weighted. Layer 4 (transport) vs Layer 7 (application) load balancing. Improves availability and performance.

Redundancy at all levels: Devices (dual switches/routers), Links (port-channel/LACP), Paths (ECMP). Failover mechanisms: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol), HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol), GLBP.
Provides automatic default gateway redundancy. Virtual IP shared among multiple routers. Master router handles traffic; backup takes over if master fails. Priority-based election (0-255).
Cisco proprietary. Similar to VRRP. Virtual IP and MAC address shared. Active router forwards; standby router takes over on failure. Uses hello and hold timers.
IEEE 802.3ad. Bundles multiple physical links into one logical link (port-channel). Increases bandwidth and provides redundancy. Requires same speed/duplex on all bundled ports.
Aggregates up to 8 parallel links. Load distribution based on source/destination MAC, IP, or port. Provides increased bandwidth and link redundancy. Uses PAGP (Cisco) or LACP (standard).
SNMP, NetFlow, sFlow, IP SLA, ICMP (ping), Syslog, NTP (synchronized timestamps for logs), LLDP/MED (device discovery and information sharing).

Synchronizes clocks across network devices. UDP port 123. Stratum levels: 0 (atomic clock), 1 (directly connected), 2-15 (lower accuracy). Important for log correlation and security certificate validation.
IEEE 802.1AB. Allows network devices to advertise their identity, capabilities, and neighbors. Used for network discovery, troubleshooting, and documenting connections. Similar to Cisco CDP.
